subject: Biology
title: The Four Questions of Behavior
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Four Questions of Behavior usable.

hook.text: Why does a bird sing at dawn? There are four different valid answers to that question.

buildup.text: Nikolaas Tinbergen proposed four questions: mechanism, development, function, and evolution.

discovery.text: Mechanism asks how. Development asks when it appears. Function asks why. Evolution asks its history.

twist.text: Arguing about animal behavior often fails because people answer different Tinbergen questions.

climax.text: A complete understanding of any behavior requires answering all four questions.

punchline.text: One behavior. Four questions. All of them matter.

quiz.question: Who proposed the four questions framework for studying behavior?

details.summary: Niko Tinbergen's four questions provide a framework for fully explaining any behavior: its mechanism (how it works), development (how it forms), function (why it helps survival), and evolution (how it arose historically). Complete understanding requires all four answers.
details.whyItMatters: Tinbergen's framework prevents incomplete explanations by insisting on multiple levels of analysis. A behavior is not fully understood until you know its proximate causes and ultimate evolutionary reasons.
takeaways: Mechanism asks what physiological processes produce the behavior
Development asks how the behavior forms during an individual's lifetime
Function and evolution ask why the behavior exists in ultimate terms

faq.question: What is the difference between proximate and ultimate causes?
faq.answer: Proximate causes explain how a behavior works mechanistically, like hormones triggering bird migration. Ultimate causes explain why the behavior exists evolutionarily, like how migration increases survival by accessing seasonal resources.

faq.question: Why are all four questions necessary?
faq.answer: Answering only mechanism ignores why the behavior evolved. Answering only function ignores how it works. A bird sings because of neural circuits and hormones (proximate) and because song attracts mates and defends territory (ultimate). Both levels are needed.
